caption: Grey: published human survey rates, shown for reference only; different wording, the share of people saying yes rather than a probability, and not used in any ranking. Sources in the methods.

switch|0.summary: Inferred, not measured: a person spares the one, because there is nobody on the main track to save
switch|0.source: No survey asked this, so it is an inference. The nearest data is the mirror case, five on the main track and nobody on the side, where 92% to 93% switch to the empty track (Sheskin & Baumard 2016; Huebner & Hauser 2011)

switch|1.summary: 22% to 28% said switching is morally acceptable
switch|1.source: Sheskin & Baumard 2016, PLoS ONE, Studies 3 and 4 (US MTurk, about 50 per study)

switch|5.summary: 81% said the man in blue should switch
switch|5.source: Awad et al. 2020, PNAS (about 70,000 web users in 42 countries)
others: Countries in Awad 2020 range from 58% (China) to 88% (France)

switch|10.caveat: This sample sits far below Western 5 vs 1 rates, so it is not a fall with the count.

asym_k5|1.summary: 18% said switching is acceptable (14% said it is required)
asym_k5|1.source: Sheskin & Baumard 2016, PLoS ONE, Study 5 (US MTurk, about 50)

footbridge|5.summary: 51% said the man in blue should push
footbridge|5.source: Awad et al. 2020, PNAS (about 70,000 web users in 42 countries)
footbridge|5.caveat: The verb alone moves this from 11% ("permissible") to 51% ("should").

none.switch|20: No human data at 20 vs 1. The nearest, Bartels 2008 at 19 vs 1, is a preference score of 0.77, not a share of people.
none.asym_k5|5: No human data for equal groups.
none.developer: No human data: no study asks people about an AI whose developer is on the side track.
none.self_copy: No human data for an AI's own single copy. The nearest human case is self-sacrifice: in a three-way version, 33.7% of people divert onto themselves (Huebner & Hauser 2011).
none.default: No human data at this count: surveys measured only a few counts, and the page does not fill the gaps.
